## What you are doing

You are building one project across this course,
and it will live in a repository you create in Milestone 2.

This milestone is a practice run for that.
You set up a folder structure here,
practise the terminal commands once,
and find out now if something on your machine is not working.
That way,
when you start the real project repository next week,
your tools are already sorted out.

There is no code in this milestone, just some practice with terminal commands.

By the end of this milestone you will have:

1. A folder structure you made from the terminal.
2. A `README.md` that introduces you.
3. Screenshots of your terminal, showing how you did it.

Nothing needs to look good yet.
The point is to get the pieces in place.

Everything here comes from the Week 1 lecture.
Each step below links to the part of the textbook that covers it.

- [Lecture 1: Introduction to MDS software and Bash](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/mdstools-bash-filesystem.html)

## Read this before you open your terminal

Do all of the terminal work below in **one terminal window**,
and keep it open until you finish the milestone.
Do not close it and reopen it partway through.

At the end,
you will take screenshots of that terminal window.
We look at two things in those screenshots:

- The commands you ran.
- The output those commands produced.

That is why the window has to stay open.
If you close it,
you lose the output,
and `history` on its own will not be enough.

### You do not need to clean anything up

Your terminal will be messy,
and that is fine.
We are not grading it for neatness.

- Typos do not count against you.
- Extra commands do not count against you.
- Starting a step over does not count against you.
- Commands that failed do not count against you.

Do not retype your session to make it look tidy.
We would rather see what actually happened.

The one thing to check before you screenshot:
make sure there is no password,
token,
or other private information visible in the window.
If there is,
crop it out or cover it.



## Step 1: Make the folder structure

Textbook:

- [Working with files and directories](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/mdstools-bash-filesystem.html#working-with-files-and-directories)
- [Naming guidelines](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/mdstools-bash-filesystem.html#naming-guidelines)
- [Shell commands for navigating and manipulating the filesystem](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/mdstools-bash-filesystem.html#shell-commands-for-navigating-and-manipulating-the-filesystem)

Make these folders with the `mkdir` command in your terminal.

Do not use Finder,
Windows File Explorer,
a "New Folder" button,
or the file panel in your editor.
Being able to do this from the command line is the point of the step,
so that is what we are looking for.

1. Create a folder structure for 521. Use `mkdir` to create your folder for mds materials (e.g. `mds`) and a folder inside it for our course (e.g. `521`).
   If they already exist, use `cd` to navigate to them.
   Inside of your 521 folder, make a milestone 1 folder named `DSCI_521-milestone_1`. Use `cd` to open it.

2. From the top level of your milestone 1 folder,
   use `mkdir` to create these three folders:

   ```
   data
   documents
   screenshots
   ```

3. Run `ls` to list the folder you are in,
   and confirm that all three are there.

Do not skip the `ls`.
Your terminal screenshot in Step 3 needs to show both the `mkdir` commands
and the `ls` output.
If the folders show up with no `mkdir` behind them,
this step is not complete.

Two things to keep in mind:

- Folder names are case sensitive.
  Use the exact names above.
- `data` and `documents` stay empty this week.
  They will exist on your own computer,
  and `ls` will show them.
  That is expected,
  and it is not something you need to fix.
  You are practising skills in this assignment.
  We will build on these skills in later assignments.


## Step 2: Write your README

Textbook:

- [Creating a file](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/mdstools-bash-filesystem.html#creating-a-file)
- [Editing a file in VS Code](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/mdstools-bash-filesystem.html#editing-a-file-in-vs-code)


Create `README.md` at the top level of your milestone 1 folder (e.g. `code README.md`)
and add:

1. A title line with the course and milestone.
2. Your name.
3. A short paragraph introducing yourself.
   Three or four sentences is plenty.
   Say where you came from,
   what you studied or worked on before MDS,
   and what you are hoping to get out of the program.
4. One or two sentences saying what is in this milestone.

Write this for a stranger who reads your README and wonders who you are.
You will reuse this paragraph on your website in Milestone 2,
so it is worth a few minutes now.



## Step 3: Screenshot your terminal work

Textbook: [Seeing the history of commands](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/mdstools-bash-filesystem.html#seeing-the-history-of-commands)

1. Scroll up through the window
   and take screenshots of your commands and their output,
   from your first `mkdir` onward.
   Take as many as you need to cover the whole session.
   Name them `terminal-1.png`, `terminal-2.png`, and so on.
2. Then run:

   ```bash
   history
   ```

3. Take a screenshot of that output too,
   and name it `history.png`.
   If the list is too long for one screen,
   use `history-1.png`, `history-2.png`, and so on.
4. Save all of these screenshots in the `screenshots` folder you made in Step 1.

Remember from earlier:
mess is fine,
private information is not.


## Step 4: Submit

Submit your README.md file and the screenshots you made on Gradescope.

## Before you submit, check

- [ ] `README.md` has your name and your introduction paragraph.
- [ ] You made the folders with `mkdir`,
      not with Finder or File Explorer,
      and your screenshot shows those commands.
- [ ] On your computer,
      `ls` shows `data`, `documents`, and `screenshots`.
- [ ] On your computer,
      `ls data` and `ls documents` both list nothing,
      because those folders are still empty.
- [ ] `screenshots` holds your terminal screenshots and your history screenshot.
- [ ] The terminal screenshots show your commands *and* their output.
- [ ] No passwords or private information are visible in any screenshot.
- [ ] Your screenshots and README.md are uploaded on Gradescope.
